title: Partition Elimination
description: YEAR()/MONTH() on a partitioned column scans every partition; a sargable date range lets the engine eliminate all but the relevant one. Why it matters: partitioning is a standard technique for very large tables in production, and knowing how to write partition-eliminating queries is essential to actually benefiting from it.
narrative:
## What This Lesson Is About
Imagine a huge archive room storing every invoice a company has ever issued, and instead of dumping every single invoice into one giant pile, someone sensibly organized them into twelve labeled boxes, one per month: 'January 2025', 'February 2025', and so on. If someone asks you to pull all the June invoices, you walk straight to the box labeled 'June 2025' and only look through that one box — you'd never waste time flipping through 'January' or 'November' looking for June invoices, because the box labels already tell you they can't possibly be in there. That's the entire idea behind **table partitioning** in SQL Server: a very large table gets physically split into separate chunks (partitions), usually by a date column, so that a query which only cares about one time range can skip straight to the relevant chunk and ignore the rest.

The magic trick that makes this actually save time is called **partition elimination**. When you write a query with a filter on the partitioning column, SQL Server's optimizer looks at your filter and compares it against the boundaries of each partition (the boxes' labels, essentially) *before* it even starts reading data. If it can mathematically prove that a partition's entire range falls outside what your filter is asking for, it skips that partition completely — never touches a single page of it. For a table split into 12 monthly partitions, a query asking for exactly one month should, in the ideal case, only ever read one-twelfth of the table. That's potentially a 12x reduction in I/O, for free, just by organizing the data sensibly and asking the right kind of question.

Here's the catch, and it's the whole point of this lesson: partition elimination only works if SQL Server can actually read the boundary being compared. It needs your filter to look like a plain, untouched comparison against the partitioning column — something like `OrderDate >= '2025-06-01' AND OrderDate < '2025-07-01'`. That's a range the optimizer can directly line up against each partition's boundary values and prove which ones can be skipped. But if you instead write `WHERE YEAR(OrderDate) = 2025 AND MONTH(OrderDate) = 6`, you've wrapped the partitioning column inside two function calls. Going back to the archive-room analogy: it's like handing the clerk a rule that says 'find every invoice where (the year the invoice was dated) equals 2025 and (the month it was dated) equals 6' instead of just saying 'June 2025 invoices.' The clerk can't map that rule onto the box labels without actually opening every box and checking every invoice inside, one at a time, computing YEAR() and MONTH() for each one — because from the optimizer's point of view, it has no general way to know in advance which raw date values would make `YEAR(OrderDate) = 2025` true without evaluating the function per row. So it falls back to reading every partition, every row, computing the function on each one to check the filter. All twelve boxes get opened and fully searched, even though a human glancing at the request would immediately know it only means one specific box.

This is really the same underlying idea as **sargability** that shows up elsewhere in SQL Server tuning (a predicate is 'sargable' — Search-ARGument-able — when it's a plain column compared to a value, letting an index or partition boundary be used directly) — it just shows up here at the partition level instead of the index-seek level. The function-wrapping mistake is an extremely common and easy one to make, because `YEAR(OrderDate) = 2025 AND MONTH(OrderDate) = 6` reads very naturally in English and is often exactly how a developer would phrase the requirement in their head. The rewrite — a half-open date range, `>= start AND < nextPeriodStart` — looks slightly less intuitive at first, but it's the version that actually lets the optimizer do its boundary math.

Why does this matter so much in production, specifically for partitioned tables? Partitioning is a standard, common technique for very large tables — often used specifically *because* a table has grown into the tens or hundreds of millions of rows and needs to be split up for manageability (partitions can be individually rebuilt, backed up, or even swapped in/out quickly) and for performance (via elimination). But partitioning by itself does nothing unless queries are actually written in a way that lets elimination kick in. A team can partition a huge table, feel good about the architecture, and then have every single report query written with `YEAR()`/`MONTH()` filters that silently defeat the entire point, scanning all partitions every time as if the table had never been partitioned at all. The scary part is that this usually doesn't throw an error or look broken — the query still returns the right answer, just after reading 12x more data than necessary, and unless someone is actually watching logical reads or partition counts in the execution plan, this can go unnoticed for a long time as 'this report is just kind of slow.'

What to look for when diagnosing this: in the execution plan, a Clustered Index Scan on a partitioned table shows an **Actual Partition Count** property — if that number equals the total number of partitions in the table when your query logically only needs one, that's the smoking gun. The fix is always the same shape: identify what date range the function-wrapped filter is really expressing, and rewrite it as a direct, half-open comparison against the raw column with no functions in the way.

## Scenario
The `Orders` table holds **1.2 million** rows for 2025, **table-partitioned by month** on `OrderDate` (12 monthly partitions). A dashboard runs a *"June revenue"* aggregate and it reads the whole table every time.

## Why it's slow
```sql
WHERE YEAR(OrderDate) = 2025 AND MONTH(OrderDate) = 6
```
Wrapping the partition key in `YEAR()`/`MONTH()` hides the date range from the optimizer. It cannot prove which partitions are relevant, so it performs **partition elimination = none** and scans **all 12 partitions** (~1.2M rows).

## The concept — partition elimination
When a predicate is a **sargable range on the partitioning column**, SQL Server compares it to the partition boundaries and **skips whole partitions** it can prove are empty of matches. A half-open month range touches exactly **one** partition:
```sql
WHERE OrderDate >= '2025-06-01' AND OrderDate < '2025-07-01'
```
Same result, ~100k rows read instead of 1.2M.

## What to look for
- Logical reads on `Orders` drop roughly **10×** (one partition vs. twelve).
- In the plan, the Clustered Index Scan's **Actual Partition Count** falls from 12 to 1. (This playground grades on logical reads, since the partition count isn't surfaced separately.)

> This lesson deliberately runs on ~1.2M rows — the scale *is* the point: partition elimination is what keeps big partitioned tables fast.
hints: YEAR()/MONTH() wrap the partitioning column, so the optimizer can't match your filter to the monthly partition boundaries — it reads all 12.
Partition elimination only kicks in for a sargable range directly on OrderDate (no functions around the column).
Rewrite as a half-open range: WHERE OrderDate >= '2025-06-01' AND OrderDate < '2025-07-01'. This touches a single partition.
